reports.goal: Retrieval-time efficiency on CPU without giving up P0 accuracy. Almost all of the per-query cost is encoding the query with F2LLM-v2-1.7B on CPU: 7.83 s mean and 8.5 GB peak RAM on Kaggle's 2-core CPU, and the author's 7.7 GiB laptop cannot run it at all. The task is to cut that cost while keeping the 1.7B document space, which is built offline where a GPU is allowed. Scope: brief ("expected on run on CPU with minimal GPU resource utilization"; the demo should show "how fast your solution is"), FAQ A ("During retrieval, you should make minimal use of the GPU (ideally use the CPU only)"), FAQ B ("relying on a large model during retrieval is not efficient"), and the FAQ's remark that the choice of model is not expected to have "a significant impact". Every candidate below changes only the query tower or the query input. Documents, execution and the frozen config stay as they are, and any new behaviour goes behind a default-off switch.
reports.landscape: Industry keeps the large document index and makes the query side cheaper. (1) Asymmetric query-encoder distillation: KALE prunes and aligns only the query encoder, with no re-indexing (https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.01016; "3x faster inference" beyond DistilBERT on MSMARCO/NQ/TriviaQA/SQuAD/SciFact). A 2-layer distilled query encoder keeps "92.5%" of the full dual encoder's BEIR performance (https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.11550). LEAF (MongoDB, ACL 2026) trains a student with an L2 loss to the teacher's vectors, without labels. In asymmetric mode leaf-ir (23M, teacher arctic-embed-m-v1.5) scores 54.8 BEIR NDCG@10, "97.7%" of the teacher (https://arxiv.org/html/2509.12539v2). (2) Unpaired space translation (vec2vec, NeurIPS 2025) reaches cosine "as high as 0.92" to the true target vectors (https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.12540). (3) CPU quantisation. Sentence-transformers reports a "4x speedup for CPU with OpenVINO int8 static quantization"; the model and dataset are not stated in the text (https://github.com/huggingface/sentence-transformers/releases/tag/v3.3.0). OpenVINO ships Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B as weight-only INT8_ASYM via nncf.compress_weights, with no accuracy figures (https://huggingface.co/OpenVINO/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B-int8-ov). Qwen ships a Q8_0 GGUF with `llama-embedding --pooling last`, also with no quantised benchmarks (https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B-GGUF). LLM.int8 explains why naive int8 fails: outlier features need mixed precision (https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.07339). (4) Neighbouring fields: the tuned lens fits an affine probe per layer to decode intermediate states (https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.08112), and "Layer by Layer" finds that intermediate layers often beat the final layer on MTEB (https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.02013). Together they suggest an early-exit query tower. The F2LLM-v2 family runs from 80M to 14B and supports Matryoshka (https://huggingface.co/codefuse-ai/F2LLM-v2-1.7B). Its card does not say that the sizes share one embedding space, and our data shows they do not.
readonly_measurements: Sanity check. scratchpad/research/qmap.py on the stored vectors, DEV all families (2,500, seed 20260919): dense 1.7B NDCG@10 0.92792 (stdin 0.90155); 0.6B 0.90056 (delta -0.02736); 160M 0.69804. All reproduce the repo's numbers.

Linear map from a small query encoder into the 1.7B document space (qmap.py; ridge regression fitted label-free on TUNE query pairs, lambda chosen by inner cross-validation; 89.6 s). For 0.6B the mapped query has DEV cosine 0.8427 to the true 1.7B vector, and NDCG@10 is 0.89618, below native 0.6B (0.90056). Fusing native and mapped scores (alpha 0.4, fitted on TUNE) gives 0.90765: +0.0071 over native 0.6B, still -0.0203 [-0.0255,-0.0153] against 1.7B. For 160M: mapped cosine 0.695, NDCG 0.714, fusion 0.755. Negative control (map fitted on shuffled pairs): 0.001, as it should. A map fitted on corpus document pairs is worse than one fitted on queries (0.6B 0.89481).

0.6B-to-1.7B cascade, replayed exactly from the outcome stores. Command: PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8 .venv/Scripts/python.exe scripts/simulate_cascade.py --small data/outcomes/f2llm06b_all_{dev,tune}_r2.jsonl.gz --large data/outcomes/f2llm17b_all_{dev,tune}.jsonl.gz, with the cost parameters set to the measured CPU seconds (2.79 and 7.83). DEV: delta -0.00182 [-0.00374,+0.00008], escalation 55.8%, encoding cost -8.6%. TUNE: delta -0.00026, escalation 57.4%, cost -7.0%. This uses the script's judge-aware policy. Side finding: the script crashes on Windows cp1252 consoles when it prints the Greek delta (Δ), unless PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8 is set.

The same cascade split by family (scratchpad/research/cascade_family.py, call-style policy, depth 20). Stdin, stop on any strong verification: DEV escalation 0.286, delta -0.00243 [-0.00709,+0.00231], 18 statements changed; TUNE escalation 0.258, delta -0.00096 [-0.00687,+0.00520], 19 changed. Estimated encoding time (from the Kaggle means) is 5.03 and 4.81 s vs 7.83 s, i.e. about 36-38% less. Other families escalate 72-74%, so the cascade costs about 7-10% more there. Stricter stop rule (the dense rank-1 verifies): stdin escalation 0.43/0.39, delta -0.0012/-0.0012.

Query length (scratchpad/research/toklen.py; tokenizer.json from the cached 0.6B snapshot, same vocab_size 151936 as the 1.7B config; the 1.7B tokenizer itself is not cached locally): DEV all families p50 330, p90 723, p99 1293 tokens, mean 397.5. DEV stdin (882) p50 498, mean 526.1. A 256-token cap keeps 47.6% of stdin tokens (91% of statements truncated); 384 keeps 67.6%; 512 keeps 82.1%.

Naive torch dynamic int8 (scratchpad/research/int8_probe.py; 0.6B on the local laptop CPU, 6 threads, 5 seeded TUNE statements, median 653 characters): fp32 2.235 s mean, cosine to the stored vectors 0.99938. int8 (torch.ao.quantize_dynamic, all nn.Linear): 1.175 s (1.9x faster), but cosine to fp32 is only 0.208 median. The encoder is destroyed. An earlier fp32 run of 15 statements measured 14.8 s/query while only 3.6 GB RAM was free, which looks like a memory-pressure artefact, so that number is not used.

Weight-only fake quantisation of the 0.6B weights, activations kept fp32 (wq_probe.py, wq_probe2.py; 8 TUNE statements; fidelity only, no speed claim). Median cosine to fp32: W8 per-channel 0.987; W8 symmetric block-32 (Q8_0-like) 0.997 (min 0.996); W8 block-128 0.995; W4 group-128 0.528; W4 block-32 0.603. Quantising one projection type at a time (W8 per-channel): q/k 0.99994, o 0.99953, gate 0.99972, up 0.99944, v 0.99763, down 0.99148, so down_proj and v_proj are the sensitive layers. Nothing reaches R2's 0.999 fidelity bar yet.

1.7B architecture (cached config.json): Qwen3Model, 28 layers, hidden size 2048, intermediate 6144, bfloat16 checkpoint. The frozen config warns that truncation under last-token pooling 'silently produces a wrong vector' when it drops the EOS token. Any cap must therefore cut the text and then append EOS.

prior_art.title: LLM.int8(): 8-bit Matrix Multiplication for Transformers at Scale
prior_art.finding: Outlier features ruin plain int8; the fix is mixed-precision decomposition (outlier dimensions kept in 16-bit).

prior_art.title: OpenVINO/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B-int8-ov
prior_art.finding: A Qwen3 embedder shipped with weight-only INT8_ASYM (nncf.compress_weights). No accuracy or speed figures.

prior_art.title: Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B-GGUF
prior_art.finding: Q8_0 GGUF, run with llama-embedding --pooling last. No quantised benchmarks.

prior_art.title: sentence-transformers v3.3.0 release

candidates.novelty_vs_trodden: R2 tried bf16 on CPU (39.4 s, fails fidelity). int8 was never tried. New here: the local probes show that the obvious route (torch dynamic int8) runs 1.9x faster but destroys the vector (cosine 0.21), and that the error sits in down_proj and v_proj. The candidate is therefore block-wise W8 with down_proj and v_proj kept in full precision (about 1/3 of the parameters, estimate from Qwen3 shapes). Asymmetric quantisation (query side only) is the design point: the document vectors are untouched.
candidates.protocol: Pre-register first. Arm A, fidelity-to-NDCG on a Kaggle T4, no fast kernel needed: fake-quantise the 1.7B weights for (i) W8 block-32 on all layers and (ii) W8 block-32 with down_proj and v_proj in fp32. Encode the 2,500 DEV and 2,500 TUNE queries with the frozen recipe and score dense NDCG@10 against the stored fp32 1.7B corpus vectors. Choose the variant on TUNE and report DEV. Then replay the pipeline, recording outcomes locally for any new top-20 documents. Arm B, speed on a Kaggle CPU kernel of the same class as R2 (2 cores, torch 2 threads): run the chosen variant through one real kernel (OpenVINO weight compression via optimum-intel, or llama.cpp Q8_0 with the sensitive tensors kept f16) on R2's seeded 100 TUNE statements. Report mean and p95 seconds, peak RAM, and cosine to the stored vectors. Arm C: repeat on the laptop, which is only possible if peak RAM stays under about 6 GB.
candidates.baseline: Dense DEV NDCG@10 0.92792 (1.7B fp32); DEV pipeline, same policy, fp32 queries; CPU 7.83 s/query mean (p95 15.7), 8.5 GB peak (R2, Kaggle 2-core).
candidates.min_effect: At least 1.5x lower mean encoding time (<= 5.2 s) with dense DEV delta >= -0.002 (non-inferior, bootstrap lower bound plus sign-flip, statements changed reported) and pipeline DEV delta >= -0.002. Secondary: peak RAM <= 6 GB, so the author's laptop can run the shipped encoder.
candidates.cost: Arm A: Kaggle T4, about 20-30 min for 5,000 queries x 2 variants (estimate); scoring offline with the stored vectors takes seconds. Arm B: Kaggle CPU, about 1-2 h including export (estimate). New pinned dependency (openvino/optimum-intel or llama-cpp-python), installed only on Kaggle until approved.
candidates.risks: R2 found bf16 slower on this Kaggle CPU, so fast int8 kernels (VNNI) may be missing too; speed is unverified. Mixed precision leaves about 1/3 of the FLOPs at fp32, capping the speedup at roughly 1.5-2x (estimate). An export path (OpenVINO or GGUF) must reproduce the EOS and last-token pooling exactly. A new runtime adds weight to the judges' MTEB re-run (FAQ), so it needs its own install check in CI. The 0.6B fidelity results may not transfer to 1.7B.
candidates.cheapest_falsifying_check: Arm A with variant (ii) on the 2,500 TUNE queries only (about 15 min on a T4). If the dense TUNE delta is below -0.005 against 0.9328-level fp32 (the TUNE number from the stored vectors), stop. Before that, locally and for free: extend wq_probe2.py to keep down/v fp32 on 0.6B and check that median cosine is >= 0.999; if it is not, stop.
candidates.expected_value: Estimate: a 1.4-2x CPU speedup at dense delta around -0.001, with P(passes both bars) about 0.4. The largest practical gain is that the shipped model runs on a 7.7 GiB machine (about 2-3 GB of weights instead of 6.9 GB).

prior_art.title: CodeDoctor V2 plan, PRE-2 (internal)
prior_art.finding: Planned, never run: encode the prose only and route the examples to the verifier; examples and notes are about 20% of characters.

prior_art.title: Query Encoder Distillation via Embedding Alignment (short query towers)
prior_art.finding: The query side tolerates heavy compression (2-layer encoder keeps 92.5% on BEIR). Evidence only that query-side information is redundant, not about truncation itself.

candidates.novelty_vs_trodden: Not tried. PRE-2 was planned at 0.6B and never run. New: measured token counts show stdin queries average 526 tokens, and a 256-token cap keeps 47.6% of them. The division of labour is intended: the encoder only has to find the right problem, and the verifier still reads the full statement. The frozen config's warning is handled by truncating the text and then appending EOS, not by lowering max_seq_length.
candidates.protocol: Pre-register first. Views: token caps of 256, 384 and 512 (text cut, EOS appended), plus the parser's prose-only view (sections before Examples). Kaggle T4: encode the 5,000 train queries per view with the frozen 1.7B recipe. Offline: dense NDCG@10 against the stored corpus vectors; choose the view on TUNE, report DEV. Then replay the call-style pipeline. Top-20 documents missing from the 1.7B and 0.6B stores are recorded locally with record_outcomes (CPU). CPU seconds per view come from one Kaggle CPU run on R2's 100 TUNE statements. Hold-out check: the CodeContests EXT-dev 1.7B stores (already adaptively reused, stated as such).
candidates.baseline: Dense DEV 0.92792 (stdin 0.90155); call-style pipeline DEV (R1); 7.83 s/query.
candidates.min_effect: Pipeline DEV delta >= -0.002 (non-inferior; sign-flip; statements changed reported) at >= 1.4x measured CPU speedup on stdin statements.
candidates.cost: Kaggle T4 about 30-40 min for 4 views x 5,000 queries (estimate; shorter inputs encode faster). Local outcome recording for the new candidates about 1 h CPU (estimate). Kaggle CPU timing about 1 h.
candidates.risks: The frozen recipe was tuned on full statements, so dense loss could be large at 256 tokens (the plan's prior: neutral to a slight loss). Execution only repairs a gold that stays in the top 20. The saving is smaller than the token share because of fixed overhead. The prose-only view depends on parser precision (0.91-0.98).
candidates.cheapest_falsifying_check: One Kaggle T4 pass encoding only the 882 DEV stdin and 825 TUNE stdin queries at cap 384 (about 5 min). If dense stdin NDCG falls by more than 0.01 on TUNE, drop caps below 512 and stop.
candidates.expected_value: Estimate: a 1.3-1.8x saving on stdin at a dense cost of -0.002 to -0.01, partly repaired by execution. P(non-inferior at >= 1.4x) about 0.3.

candidates.name: C3: Early-exit 1.7B query tower: layer-k last-token state plus an affine head into the final space (tuned-lens idea)
candidates.scope_goal: CPU efficiency at retrieval with the 1.7B document space kept
candidates.scope_quote: The theme focuses on pre/post processing and we don't expect the choice of a embedding/retrieval model to have a significant impact.

prior_art.title: Eliciting Latent Predictions from Transformers with the Tuned Lens
prior_art.finding: An affine probe per layer decodes intermediate hidden states of frozen LMs (up to 20B) better than the logit lens.

prior_art.title: Layer by Layer: Uncovering Hidden Representations in Language Models
prior_art.finding: On MTEB, intermediate layers often outperform the final layer ('2% to 16% on average', as summarised by the search result; the PDF was not read in full, so this figure is unverified).

prior_art.title: KALE
prior_art.finding: Pruning only the query encoder's layers, then aligning it to the frozen original, keeps the index; about 3x faster inference.

candidates.novelty_vs_trodden: Not tried. It differs from the trodden cross-model routes because the head maps within one model's residual stream, not between models. Our cross-model linear map measured cosine 0.84 and NDCG below native 0.6B, which is the warning; states at layers 20-24 are hypothesised (unverified) to be much closer to the final vector. It needs no training beyond a closed-form ridge fit.
candidates.protocol: Pre-register first. Kaggle T4, one pass: encode the 5,000 train queries with the frozen recipe and output_hidden_states. Store the last-token states for layers {16, 20, 24} (5,000 x 2,048 x 3 in float32, about 120 MB). Offline: fit ridge maps from layer-k state to the final normalised embedding on TUNE (label-free, like qmap.py), then score dense DEV NDCG@10 against the stored corpus. Controls: the identity check at layer 28 must reproduce 0.92792, and the shuffled-pair map must collapse (both already exercised in qmap.py). If k <= 20 passes, measure CPU seconds on Kaggle CPU with a truncated model (layers 0..k-1 plus head).
candidates.min_effect: At k = 20 (about 29% fewer layer FLOPs; estimate, excluding embedding and head) the dense DEV delta is >= -0.002. At k = 24, a delta >= -0.002 would be worth only about 14% (descriptive).
candidates.cost: Kaggle T4 about 15 min (estimate); offline fits in seconds to minutes on the laptop from the stored arrays.
candidates.risks: The largest plausible saving is 30-45%, less than C1. Near the top layers, last-token pooling may depend on late-layer mixing, and the head can overfit 2,500 TUNE pairs in 2,048-d, which is why the fit uses ridge. It stacks with C1 and C2 but multiplies the switches.
candidates.cheapest_falsifying_check: The same Kaggle pass with layer 24 only. If the ridge-mapped DEV dense delta at layer 24 is below -0.005, lower layers will not pass either, so kill the idea.
candidates.expected_value: Estimate: P(k = 20 non-inferior) about 0.25; if it passes, about 1.3-1.4x faster. Low cost to learn.

prior_art.finding: 160M-to-0.6B was rejected (-0.0076, escalation 62%). 0.6B-to-1.7B was only estimated (about 20% saving on stdin).

candidates.novelty_vs_trodden: The trodden cascade used different tiers (160M first). What is new is that 0.6B-to-1.7B has now been replayed exactly from the R1/R2 stores. Over all families it saves only 7-9%, but on stdin only 26-29% of statements escalate, an estimated 36-38% encoding saving. Routing by family uses query text only (allowed).
candidates.protocol: Measured in-sample on both halves, so these numbers are descriptive, not a pass. Pre-register the rule (stdin: stop on any strong verification; other families go straight to 1.7B), then test it once on the CodeContests EXT-dev stores (f2llm06b_extcc_dev_deep50 vs f2llm17b_extcc_dev; adaptively reused, stated as such). Measure real serial latency on Kaggle CPU, because escalated queries pay 0.6B encoding, execution and 1.7B encoding in sequence.
candidates.baseline: 1.7B call-style pipeline on DEV stdin (replayed); 7.83 s/query mean.
candidates.min_effect: Stdin pipeline delta >= -0.002 (non-inferior) with a measured mean-latency saving >= 25%.
candidates.cost: Offline replay takes seconds to minutes (done). Latency needs Kaggle CPU about 1 h. RAM: both models resident, about 3.9 + 8.5 GB (worse than today).
candidates.risks: DEV stdin delta -0.0024 [-0.0071,+0.0023] does not show non-inferiority. p95 latency is unchanged or worse for escalated queries. It keeps the 1.7B in RAM, so it does not help the laptop. It relies on the verifier, whose value shrinks on small pools (P0 ceiling result). Arguably it goes against the spirit of FAQ B, since the large model still runs for about 28% of queries.
candidates.cheapest_falsifying_check: Replay on the EXT-dev stores. If stdin escalation is > 50% or delta < -0.005, kill it.
candidates.expected_value: Estimate: about 1.3-1.5x mean encoding saving on stdin, at about -0.001 to -0.002 NDCG. The weakest of the four; it stacks with C1 only if C1 fails.

rejected.name: Linear/orthogonal (Procrustes-style) map from the 0.6B or 160M query space into the 1.7B document space
rejected.reason: Measured offline (qmap.py). 0.6B mapped: 0.89618, worse than native 0.6B (0.90056). 160M mapped: 0.714. Fusing native and mapped: 0.90765, still -0.0203 against 1.7B. A paired map is the most information such a method can use, so unpaired variants cannot do better.

rejected.name: vec2vec-style unpaired translation
rejected.reason: Strictly less information than the paired ridge map, which already fails. The paper's best cosine is 0.92 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.12540), and our paired 0.84 already costs more NDCG than using native 0.6B.

rejected.name: LEAF/KALE-style trained student into the 1.7B space (0.6B or smaller student)
rejected.reason: The industry-standard answer, but the arithmetic is poor here. LEAF's asymmetric student keeps about 97.7% of its teacher (BEIR). 97.7% of 0.928 is about 0.907, the native 0.6B level we already have. Beating that needs a student of about 0.6B size (2.79 s), and GPU training on APPS train text brings overfitting risk (FAQ 4). Revisit only if C1-C3 all fail.

rejected.name: torch dynamic int8 (per-tensor activations)
rejected.reason: Measured on 0.6B: 1.9x faster but cosine 0.21 to fp32. The vector is destroyed (outlier activations, cf. LLM.int8).

rejected.name: int4 weight-only (RTN group-32 or group-128)
rejected.reason: Measured fake-quant cosine 0.53-0.60 on 0.6B. Calibrated methods (AWQ/GPTQ) would need GPU calibration and start from a very large fidelity gap.

rejected.name: 0.6B-to-1.7B cascade over all families
rejected.reason: Measured replay: 56-57% escalation and only a 7-9% encoding saving. It costs more on call-style families (72-74% escalate).

rejected.name: Matryoshka dimension truncation
rejected.reason: Only cuts the scoring and storage cost (8,765 x 2,048 dot products take milliseconds), not query encoding, which is the actual cost.

rejected.name: bf16 on CPU, batching, 160M-to-0.6B cascade, plain 0.6B swap
rejected.reason: Already measured (39.4 s and failed fidelity; batching slower; -0.0076; -0.0169 on the pipeline). Nothing new would change those outcomes.

rejected.name: Query-time LLM or API (HyDE, rerankers), GPU at query time
rejected.reason: Out of scope under FAQ A and B.

rejected.name: ONNX Runtime fp32 graph optimisation alone
rejected.reason: The gain is unverified and likely small for a compute-bound 1.7B decoder. At most a control arm inside C1, not a separate experiment.

reports.goal: P0 retrieval accuracy (NDCG@10/MRR) that transfers to the judges' unseen Python dataset, which the FAQ calls "representative of the APPS dataset". The gain has to come from pre/post-processing that also generalises, not from APPS-specific tuning, and query time has to stay on CPU.
reports.landscape:
For NL-to-code retrieval where query time must stay cheap, the usual expert answer is a strong embedder plus offline document enrichment (LLM summaries or doc2query), then execution- or test-based selection.

Offline enrichment gains shrink or vanish with strong embedders:
- EnrichIndex (https://arxiv.org/html/2504.03598) reports +10.6 NDCG@10 on average. Its strongest hybrid, BM25+Snowflake on BRIGHT, gains only 33.0 -> 34.7. Its retrievers are small encoders, not LLM embedders.
- CodeBridge (https://arxiv.org/html/2504.07740) tests only SQL, Solidity and CoSQA, not APPS, with small PLMs (UniXcoder, CoCoSoDa). LLM-based embeddings (DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B) "perform very poorly" there.
- Tool-retrieval document expansion (https://arxiv.org/html/2510.22670v1, Table 2 as read by the fetch tool): Qwen3-Embedding-8B 46.21 -> 46.23, e5-mistral-7b 40.02 -> 38.85.

TACO (https://arxiv.org/html/2312.14852v3) confirms two things about APPS-style data. CodeChef content comes in "multiple HTML syntax formats" (line breaks included), and APPS tests have a false-positive rate "up to 60%".

The Python docs (https://docs.python.org/3/library/constants.html) confirm that `-S` suppresses `site`, which is what adds `exit` and `quit` to builtins.

Going deeper, the most useful adjacent field was judge fidelity: run candidates the way a judge would, and canonicalise rendering artefacts. That is not another re-ranking rule. It fits RESULTS lesson 1 ("adding evidence worked; re-reading evidence did not"). Our data shows the verifier cannot see the gold at all on a measurable share of statements, for reasons unrelated to relevance.
readonly_measurements: Loss decomposition, replay of call-style+deep50 on data/outcomes/f2llm17b_all_{dev,tune}_deep50.jsonl.gz (scratchpad/research/decompose.py, stdin_decomp.py). All-family NDCG@10: DEV 0.95327, TUNE 0.95849. Stdin family: DEV 0.95993 (dense 0.90155), TUNE 0.96362. Largest all-family loss class: no parsed examples, so no execution. DEV 1,013/2,500 statements, 0.0198 of the 0.0467 loss, mostly kata. Stdin DEV loss per stdin statement 0.0401: gold crashes with nothing verified 0.0080; gold beyond top-50 0.0079; gold verified but another verified above 0.0060.

Blank-line sample inputs (prevalence.py): 35/824 DEV and 24/777 TUNE stdin statements have sample inputs with every other line blank. Only 1 of each set gets any verification. Gold crashes in 29/35 (DEV) and 20/24 (TUNE). Pipeline NDCG on them: DEV 0.740, TUNE 0.852.

Live TUNE-only check, blank lines collapsed (blank_check.py, 31.8 s, 480 runs): gold verifies in 21/24. Non-gold verifications: 9 across 4 statements. NDCG on the 24 statements 0.8520 -> 0.9638. Effect: +0.0033 on TUNE stdin, +0.0011 on all TUNE. DEV was not touched.

Expected-output trailing-prose trim, TUNE replay (prose.py): 16 statements trimmed, 11 golds newly verified, 3 non-gold newly verified, 0 verifications lost. Only 1 statement's NDCG changes: stdin +0.00081 [0, +0.00242].

EXT-dev gold crashes (ext.py, fidelity.py): 9/107 executed golds crash. 6 use `io.BytesIO(os.read(0, os.fstat(0).st_size))` fast IO; 3 call bare `exit()` (NameError under -S). Live re-run with stdin as a file plus `exit = quit = sys.exit`: 7/9 golds MATCH. cc-test-156 still crashes; it has blank-line input. Negative control: non-gold top-10 candidates verify 13/81 under pipe and 13/81 after the change. The 9 statements carry 0.0296 of EXT-dev loss (pipeline 0.75431).

APPS prevalence of those idioms: 17/8,765 corpus docs use bare exit/quit, 24 use fast IO. Gold crashes from a missing numpy (the -S sandbox has no site-packages): DEV 3, TUNE 11, loss about 0.0004 on TUNE.
Dense Rocchio PRF on TUNE with stored vectors (prf.py): 1.7B baseline 0.93779. Every setting is worse: k=1, beta=0.1 gives 0.93696; k=5, beta=0.5 gives 0.92767. 0.6B is also worse at every setting.

reports.goal: P1: rebuild indexes and caches after any version or change in a reasonable time. The FAQ allows incremental or full rebuilds but says "we would consider the time and resource utilization during the evalution", and allows the GPU "during pre/post processing (including incremental updates)". Bonus: "retrieve code snippets across all versions", where versions "would still be very similar, which would make them hard to rank properly". Both are judged hands-on, on an unseen Python dataset "representative of the APPS dataset", so the FAQ's advice against overfitting to APPS applies. The FAQ does not say how the Bonus is scored or what a "version" will look like in the unseen set. Nothing in this cycle touches the P0 screening score.
reports.landscape:
P1, what industry does. Production tools content-address the corpus and re-embed only what changed.
- Cursor hashes every file into a Merkle tree and caches embeddings by chunk content. Reusing an index cuts median time-to-first-query "from 7.87 seconds to 525 milliseconds" (https://cursor.com/blog/secure-codebase-indexing).
- GitHub's Blackbird shards the index by git blob ID. "Content deduplication and delta indexing" cut 115 TB to about 28 TB of unique content, and delta indexing halves re-crawl (18 h against 36 h) (https://github.blog/engineering/architecture-optimization/the-technology-behind-githubs-new-code-search/).
- CodeDoctor already does this (sha256 per file and per chunk in `app/indexing/incremental.py`, a recipe-keyed corpus cache in `app/pipeline/encoder.py`, content addressing in `lineage.py`). This path is trodden. What is missing is measurement, plus one cache-key defect.

Bonus, prior art.
- ExecRetrieval found embeddings rank the canonical code below a single-edit buggy clone in 67–78% of queries (https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01865).
- Outside retrieval, the tools for telling near-identical programs apart are:
  - extra inputs from type-aware mutation (EvalPlus: 80x more HumanEval tests, pass@k down 19.3–28.9%; https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.01210);
  - choosing by execution agreement without ground-truth outputs (MBR-exec, https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.11454; CodeT dual agreement, 65.8% pass@1 on HumanEval, https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.10397);
  - patch-correctness assessment in program repair, which is the closest analogue because overfitting patches pass the given tests (PATCH-SIM blocked 56.3% of incorrect patches and no correct ones, https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.09120v2; RGT uses a ground-truth reference, https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.13694).

All of these need either an oracle or independent errors. My pilot suggests the missing oracle is the limit, not the lack of inputs.

candidates.protocol: Pre-register first. Seed the scored-path corpus cache from the stored GPU vectors (8,765 documents). Apply change sets taken from the versions_apps single-edit mutants: 1, 10, 100 and 450 changed snippets, plus one 10%-replacement batch. Run 0.6B on this laptop (6 threads) and 1.7B on the codedoctor-cpu-bench Kaggle CPU kernel (2 cores, as in R2). Also run an all-GPU-vector control and an all-CPU-vector control to size the mixed-origin rank-flip rate. Controls: (a) sanity: reproduce 1.18 s per document at 0.6B within 15%; (b) negative: change the document prefix; the scored path must miss 100%. The version-difference part is query-independent, so it can be computed at index time as P1 pre-processing.
candidates.protocol: Pre-register first. Build E5-hard on DEV (the pilot used TUNE): gold plus up to 3 single-edit mutants that pass the worked examples but fail APPS official tests. Official tests are the judge only; the pipeline never sees them. Target about 150 lineages. Encode the new versions for dense scores on Kaggle T4 (1.7B, fp16) or reuse the build script. Arms: (1) the shipped rule (verified first, then dense order); (2) plus MBR-exec among verified versions using 24 integer-mutated sample inputs, counting only inputs where most versions run, with dense order breaking ties. Metrics: exec@1, buggy_above, and share of lineages with a distinguishing input found. Paired bootstrap plus sign-flip test, Holm correction. Controls: (a) replaying E5 must still give 0.953, since the rule only acts inside ties; (b) negative control: official inputs with outputs shuffled across versions must give chance; (c) a correlated-history arm (mutant A, mutant A plus an equivalent edit, gold) where MBR is predicted to pick the buggy majority, reported as a limit.

candidates.min_effect: At least +0.10 absolute exec@1 over the shipped rule on E5-hard, with the interval excluding zero and sign-flip p < 0.05, from 15 or more changed lineages, and no change on E5.
candidates.cost: Laptop CPU: about 10k sandbox runs, around 8 min with 6 workers. A T4 encode of about 450 new versions takes about 1 min.
candidates.risks: Real version histories share bugs (a bug introduced and carried until fixed), so majority voting then picks the bug; the correlated arm quantifies this. Integer-only mutation can create invalid inputs (handled by the majority-runs filter). With 2-version lineages MBR can only tie. Single-edit mutants are synthetic, and the FAQ says nothing about what versions the hands-on uses.
candidates.cheapest_falsifying_check: Already run as a pilot on TUNE. Kill rule: if MBR using official inputs (the ceiling) is at most chance + 0.05, stop. Measured 0.465 against 0.326, so the idea survives, but the ceiling is low: better inputs do not help much (0.460 generated vs 0.465 official), so the oracle, not the inputs, is the bottleneck.
candidates.expected_value: Estimate: +0.10 to +0.15 exec@1 on sample-passing lineages (pilot +0.13 over chance, n=33, no interval). No effect on the P0 APPS score, which has no version lineages. It also yields a demo-able witness input ('v2 prints 5, v3 prints 6 on this input') for about 60% of near-misses.

candidates.name: Bonus-B: the same tie-break on real near-identical submissions (CodeContests EXT-dev incorrect submissions)
candidates.scope_quote: FAQ: your approach should ideally generalize and not overfit on a dataset / brief: very similar, which would make them hard to rank properly

prior_art.title: MBR-exec
prior_art.finding: Execution-agreement selection without reference outputs

prior_art.title: Automated Patch Assessment for Program Repair at Scale (RGT)
prior_art.finding: Tests generated from a ground-truth reference identify overfitting patches (638 Defects4J patches); needs a known-correct reference, which retrieval lacks

candidates.novelty_vs_trodden: E3 showed that 62 of 66 rank-1 errors were incorrect submissions to the same problem and that samples cannot separate them. No new evidence has been tried on them since; E8 rejected 1 of 111. These are human bugs, which may be more independent than mutants and so suit MBR better, or more correlated through shared misconceptions, which would hurt it.
candidates.protocol: Pre-register first. EXT-dev only (108 statements; never the lockbox). For each statement whose top 20 holds 2 or more sample-verified candidates, run the verified candidates on 24 type-aware mutated sample inputs, then reorder only within the verified tier by MBR score, with dense order breaking ties. Compare NDCG@10 and gold-first-within-tie against the recorded call-style replay. Paired bootstrap, sign-flip test, count of changed statements. Stop after 10 min of CPU.
candidates.baseline: 1.7B EXT-dev call-style NDCG@10 0.7589; within verified ties dense already puts the gold first 29/58 = 0.500 (chance 0.349); ceiling 0.8702 (+0.111, 29 reachable statements). All measured read-only today.
candidates.min_effect: Gold-first within ties of 0.60 or more (6 or more net statements) and an NDCG gain with an interval excluding zero; any loss on the 29 ties dense already gets right counts against it.
candidates.cost: Laptop CPU: about 58 statements x 3.5 verified x 24 inputs, roughly 5k runs, about 5 min. No GPU.
candidates.risks: Multiple comparisons on a reused EXT-dev set, and n = 58 ties is underpowered for small effects. Some incorrect submissions are wrong only on time limits, so their outputs match the gold on small inputs and give no signal. 47 of 108 statements come from the valid split (contamination is plausible but unverified).
candidates.cheapest_falsifying_check: Run MBR on the first 20 tie statements (about 1 min). If gold-first within ties is 0.50 or less, the dense order it would replace, kill it. The mutant pilot's MBR (0.46) sits below this bar, so the prior is that it fails.
candidates.expected_value: Estimate: -0.02 to +0.03 NDCG@10 on EXT-dev; likely null. It is worth running because it is the realistic test of whether Bonus-A generalises beyond synthetic mutants, and a null result bounds what the Bonus can claim.

rejected.name: Merkle tree over directories (Cursor-style) for change detection
rejected.reason: The repo already hashes every file and chunk with sha256 and caches vectors by content. A Merkle tree only speeds up detecting changes, which costs milliseconds, while embedding costs about 1.2 s per snippet. A snippet corpus like APPS has no directory tree anyway. Trodden, with no measurable gain.

rejected.name: Reuse the previous version's vector for near-identical edits (lazy re-embedding)
rejected.reason: Measured today: unconditional reuse costs lineage@1 0.853 -> 0.833 at 1.7B (3 of 150 lineages) and saves about 1.2 s of CPU per changed snippet. That is a real correctness loss for a saving the FAQ's time criterion does not need; a Jaccard-gated variant would still need texts that are not stored locally.

rejected.name: Length-sorted batching for CPU document encoding
rejected.reason: Already in `app/retrieval/encode.py:plan_batches`. R2 measured batching slower than batch 1 on CPU (15.3 s vs 7.8 s per query at 1.7B).

rejected.name: bfloat16 or int8 quantisation for CPU re-indexing
rejected.reason: R2 measured bfloat16 as slower (39.4 s vs 7.83 s) and failing the 0.999 fidelity bar. int8 is an unverified speedup that would change query vectors on the scored path. It needs its own fidelity pre-registration and is a P0 risk, not a P1 lever.

rejected.name: LLM-generated tests at query time (CodeT-style)
rejected.reason: FAQ: 'Usage of an API during the retrieval also counts as utilizing the GPU' and a large model per query 'is not efficient'. The query-independent part (inputs that separate versions) is folded into Bonus-A as index-time work instead.

rejected.name: Metamorphic relations and judge-aware comparator for near-misses
rejected.reason: Trodden. E8 rejected 1 of 111 real near-misses; the judge-aware comparator gave +0.0004 at 1.7B. Neither adds new evidence.

rejected.name: PATCH-SIM execution-trace similarity
rejected.reason: Needs instrumentation and a passing/failing test split that a query does not provide. The cheaper output-level differential in Bonus-A covers the same idea.

rejected.name: RGT-style reference-based differential testing
rejected.reason: Needs a known-correct reference version, which does not exist at query time.

rejected.name: 'Latest version wins' recency prior as the primary Bonus rule
rejected.reason: The FAQ does not say how the hands-on versions are ordered. E5 randomises the correct version's position on purpose, and lineage.py already uses recency only as the last tie-break. Promoting it would be a guess about the judge's data.

rejected.name: Consensus with other correct solutions of the same problem in the corpus
rejected.reason: The APPS corpus holds one solution per problem, and the unseen set is 'representative of the APPS dataset', so there is usually nothing to agree with outside the lineage.
